topics.title: Object.groupBy and Map.groupBy (ES2024)
topics.summary: Group an iterable by a key function natively, returning either a plain null-prototype object or a Map.
topics.description:
**Support:** ES2024. Available in Node 21+, Chrome 117+, Firefox 119+, Safari 17.4+. Older runtimes need a `reduce` fallback.

`Object.groupBy(items, callback)` loops over any iterable, calls `callback(item, index)` to get a key, and returns an object whose properties are arrays of the items sharing that key. `Map.groupBy` does the same but returns a `Map`, so keys can be **any value** (objects, numbers, booleans) instead of being converted to strings.

### Key facts
| | `Object.groupBy` | `Map.groupBy` |
|---|---|---|
| Result | object with `null` prototype | `Map` |
| Key types | strings or symbols (others converted) | any value, compared with SameValueZero |
| Key order | insertion order, but integer-like keys come first | insertion order |
| Use for | JSON-like output | numeric/object keys, ordered results |

- The object has **no prototype**, so keys like `toString` or `constructor` are safe, but you cannot call `result.hasOwnProperty()`. Use `Object.hasOwn(result, key)`.
- Groups keep the original item order.
- Works with arrays, Sets, generators and other iterables.
- It does not mutate the input and does not copy items (shallow references).

### Replaces
The classic `reduce` pattern: `arr.reduce((g, x) => ((g[f(x)] ??= []).push(x), g), {})`. The native method is shorter and avoids prototype-pollution pitfalls with keys such as `__proto__`.

### Typical uses
Group orders by status, products by category, events by day, or bucket numbers into ranges (return a label from the callback).
keyPoints: Object.groupBy returns a null-prototype object of arrays; Map.groupBy returns a Map.
Use Map.groupBy when keys are not strings.
The callback receives (item, index).
Group order inside each bucket matches the original order.
Standardised in ES2024; older engines need a fallback.
pitfalls: Calling result.hasOwnProperty fails because the object has no prototype.
Integer-like keys in an object are reordered to the front regardless of insertion order.

examples.title: Grouping with both APIs

interview.q: Why does Object.groupBy return an object with a null prototype?
interview.a: So that group names like constructor or __proto__ cannot clash with inherited properties.

interview.q: When would you use Map.groupBy instead?
interview.a: When the grouping key is not a string, such as a number, boolean or object, or when you want guaranteed insertion order.

topics.title: Non-mutating Array Methods: toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with (ES2023)
topics.summary: Copy-then-change array methods plus findLast, at and flat tools that make immutable updates easy.
topics.description:
**Support:** ES2023. Node 20+, Chrome 110+, Firefox 115+, Safari 16+. TypedArrays have `toSorted`, `toReversed` and `with` too.

The old `sort`, `reverse` and `splice` mutate the original array, which causes bugs in React state, Redux reducers and shared data. ES2023 adds **change-by-copy** versions that return a modified copy and leave the source untouched.

| Mutating | Copying version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `arr.sort(cmp)` | `arr.toSorted(cmp)` | still needs a comparator for numbers |
| `arr.reverse()` | `arr.toReversed()` | |
| `arr.splice(i, d, ...items)` | `arr.toSpliced(i, d, ...items)` | returns the **new array**, not the removed items |
| `arr[i] = v` | `arr.with(i, v)` | throws `RangeError` if the index is out of range |

### Related search helpers
- `findLast(fn)` and `findLastIndex(fn)` (ES2023) search from the end.
- `at(-1)` (ES2022) reads from the end.
- `Array.prototype.group` was **not** shipped; use `Object.groupBy`.

### Sparse arrays
The copying methods read holes as `undefined` and always produce dense arrays.

### Remember
These make a **shallow** copy: objects inside are still shared. They are O(n) per call, so avoid in tight loops over huge arrays; use them where clarity and immutability matter.
keyPoints: toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with return new arrays and leave the source unchanged.
toSpliced returns the modified copy, unlike splice which returns removed items.
with(i, v) replaces one element immutably and throws RangeError for invalid indexes.
findLast and findLastIndex search from the end.
Copies are shallow; nested objects are shared.
pitfalls: toSorted without a comparator still sorts numbers as strings.
Old runtimes (Node 18 and below) lack these methods; polyfill or transpile.

examples.title: Immutable updates

interview.q: What does toSpliced return compared with splice?
interview.a: toSpliced returns the new modified array without changing the original; splice mutates and returns the removed elements.

interview.q: Why are these methods useful in React?
interview.a: State must not be mutated; copying methods allow sorting or updating items without touching the previous state object.

topics.title: Promise.withResolvers, Promise.try, Array.fromAsync
topics.summary: Newer async helpers that remove boilerplate: externally resolved promises, safe sync-or-async wrapping, and collecting async iterables.
topics.description:
### Promise.withResolvers (ES2024)
Before: `let resolve, reject; const promise = new Promise((res, rej) => { resolve = res; reject = rej; });`
Now: `const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();`. Great for turning event callbacks, queues and "wait until X happens" flows into promises. Node 22+, modern browsers.

### Promise.try (ES2025)
`Promise.try(fn, ...args)` runs `fn` immediately (synchronously) and returns a promise. A synchronous throw becomes a rejection, and a normal return value (or returned promise) is wrapped. It fixes the classic bug where `new Promise(r => r(fn()))` or `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` either delays the call or leaks sync errors. Available in Node 24 (V8 12.8+) and current browsers.

### Array.fromAsync
`await Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable, mapFn)` collects an async iterable (or a sync iterable of promises) into an array. It awaits each element **sequentially**, unlike `Promise.all(array)`. Shipped in all current engines since about 2023-24 (Node 22+).

### Related existing features
- `Promise.any`, `allSettled` (ES2020-21) and `for await...of` (ES2018).
- `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` and `AbortSignal.any([...])` for cancellation (web platform, Node 20+).
- `await` at the top level of modules (ES2022).

### Use cases
Test helpers, deferred values, event-to-promise adapters, wrapping library functions that may be sync or async, and reading streams into arrays.
keyPoints: Promise.withResolvers returns { promise, resolve, reject } without an executor closure.
Promise.try turns synchronous throws into rejections and runs the function immediately.
Array.fromAsync collects async iterables into an array, awaiting sequentially.
All three are available in Node 24 and current evergreen browsers.
AbortSignal.timeout complements them for cancellation.
pitfalls: Promise.try calls the function synchronously, unlike Promise.resolve().then(fn).
Array.fromAsync is sequential; use Promise.all for parallel awaiting.

examples.title: Deferred, try and fromAsync

interview.q: What problem does Promise.try solve?
interview.a: It lets you start a function that may be sync or async and always get a promise, with synchronous exceptions converted to rejections, while still running the function immediately.

interview.q: How does Array.fromAsync differ from Promise.all?
interview.a: fromAsync consumes an async iterable one element at a time; Promise.all awaits an existing array of promises concurrently.

topics.title: Set Methods: union, intersection, difference and more (ES2025)
topics.summary: Seven new Set methods that finally give set algebra natively, with notes on set-like arguments and support.
topics.description:
**Support:** ES2025. Node 22+, Chrome 122+, Firefox 127+, Safari 17+.

Before ES2025 you had to write `new Set([...a].filter(x => b.has(x)))`. Now `Set.prototype` has:

| Method | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `a.union(b)` | new Set | in a or b |
| `a.intersection(b)` | new Set | in both |
| `a.difference(b)` | new Set | in a but not b |
| `a.symmetricDifference(b)` | new Set | in exactly one |
| `a.isSubsetOf(b)` | boolean | every item of a is in b |
| `a.isSupersetOf(b)` | boolean | a contains every item of b |
| `a.isDisjointFrom(b)` | boolean | no shared items |

### Details
- Methods are **non-mutating**; they return a new `Set` and leave both inputs alone.
- The argument only needs to be **set-like**: an object with `size`, `has()` and `keys()`. A `Map` qualifies (its keys are used), an `Array` does **not** and throws a `TypeError`.
- The result order follows spec rules (items from `a` first for union; for `intersection` order depends on which set is smaller).
- Equality is SameValueZero: `NaN` equals `NaN`, objects by reference.

### Use cases
Permissions (`required.isSubsetOf(granted)`), tag filtering, diffing selected ids, removing duplicates between lists.

### Not included
There is no in-place mutation variant (no `unionWith`); use `for (const x of b) a.add(x)` for that.
keyPoints: Seven new methods: union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, isDisjointFrom.
They return new Sets; they never mutate.
The argument must be set-like (size, has, keys); arrays are rejected.
A Map can be passed as a set-like argument.
Part of ES2025 and available in Node 22+.
pitfalls: Passing an array throws a TypeError; wrap it with new Set(array).
Do not depend on exact result ordering of intersection across engines.

examples.title: Set algebra

interview.q: Do the new Set methods mutate the Set?
interview.a: No. They return a new Set (or a boolean for the is* methods) and leave the originals unchanged.

interview.q: What does set-like mean for the argument?
interview.a: An object with a numeric size property and has() and keys() methods; arrays do not qualify.

topics.title: Iterator Helpers: map, filter, take, drop, flatMap, toArray (ES2025)
topics.summary: Lazy array-like methods on iterators and generators, so you can process infinite or huge sequences without building arrays.
topics.description:
**Support:** ES2025. Node 22+ (V8 12+), Chrome 122+, Firefox 131+, Safari 18.4+.

Arrays have `map` and `filter`, but iterators (generators, `Map.prototype.entries()`, `Set.prototype.values()`...) did not. ES2025 adds a global `Iterator` and these methods on `Iterator.prototype`:

| Method | Returns | Lazy? |
|---|---|---|
| `map(fn)`, `filter(fn)` | iterator | yes |
| `take(n)`, `drop(n)` | iterator | yes |
| `flatMap(fn)` | iterator (fn returns an iterable) | yes |
| `toArray()` | array | consumes |
| `forEach(fn)` | undefined | consumes |
| `reduce(fn, init)` | value | consumes |
| `some`, `every`, `find` | boolean / item | stops early |
| `Iterator.from(x)` | wraps any iterable or iterator | - |

### Why lazy matters
`naturals().filter(isEven).map(square).take(3).toArray()` processes only as many numbers as needed, even though `naturals()` is infinite. With arrays you would need the whole array first.

### Details
- Each helper returns a new iterator that is itself iterable and has the helpers, so chains work.
- Callbacks receive `(value, counter)`.
- Values are consumed once; an iterator cannot be rewound.
- `take`, `find`, `some` and `every` call `return()` on the source to release resources.
- Async iterator helpers are a separate proposal and are **not** available yet.
- `Iterator` can be extended: `class MyIt extends Iterator { next() {...} }` gains all helpers.
keyPoints: Iterator helpers run lazily and process one item at a time through the chain.
take and drop let you slice infinite generators.
toArray, forEach, reduce, some, every and find consume the iterator.
Iterator.from wraps plain iterators so they gain the helper methods.
Async iterator helpers are not part of ES2025.
pitfalls: An iterator is exhausted after one pass; calling toArray twice gives an empty array the second time.
Helpers are not available on arrays themselves; call arr.values() first.

examples.title: Lazy pipeline over an infinite generator

interview.q: What is the advantage of iterator helpers over array methods?
interview.a: They are lazy: they pull one value at a time, so you can work with infinite generators and avoid creating intermediate arrays.

interview.q: Can you reuse an iterator after toArray()?
interview.a: No, iterators are single-pass; after being consumed they are done.

topics.title: Modern RegExp: v flag, duplicate named groups, inline modifiers, RegExp.escape
topics.summary: Newer regex features: unicodeSets (v), set subtraction and intersection, duplicate named groups, (?i:) modifiers, and RegExp.escape.
topics.description:
Regex gained several features after named groups and lookbehind (ES2018). Check engine support in older environments.

| Feature | Version | Node 24 |
|---|---|---|
| `d` flag (match indices) | ES2022 | yes |
| `v` flag (unicodeSets) | ES2024 | yes |
| Duplicate named groups (in different alternatives) | ES2025 | yes |
| Inline modifiers `(?i:...)`, `(?-i:...)` | ES2025 | yes |
| `RegExp.escape(str)` | ES2025 | yes (V8 13.6) |

### The `v` flag
An upgrade to `u`. In a character class you can use:
- **Set subtraction**: `[\p{L}--[a-z]]` letters except lowercase ASCII.
- **Intersection**: `[\p{Script=Greek}&&\p{Letter}]`.
- **Nested classes**: `[[a-z]--[aeiou]]` consonants.
- **String properties** such as `\p{RGI_Emoji}` (matches whole emoji sequences).
- Stricter syntax: characters like `(`, `)`, `[`, `{`, `}`, `/`, `-`, `|` must be escaped inside classes.
You cannot combine `u` and `v`.

### Duplicate named groups
`/(?<y>\d{4})-\d\d|\d\d-(?<y>\d{4})/` lets the same name appear in different alternatives; whichever branch matched fills `groups.y`.

### Modifiers
`(?i:abc)def` makes only `abc` case-insensitive; `(?-i:...)` turns it off inside an `i` regex. Supported flags: `i`, `m`, `s`.

### RegExp.escape
Escapes text so it can be used literally in a regex: `new RegExp(RegExp.escape(userInput))`. Replaces homemade escapers.

### Also useful
The `d` flag gives `match.indices` with start/end positions for every group.
keyPoints: The v flag adds set subtraction (--), intersection (&&) and emoji string properties.
Duplicate named groups are allowed in separate alternatives.
(?i:...) applies a flag to only part of a pattern.
RegExp.escape safely escapes user text for literal matching.
u and v cannot be used together.
pitfalls: Under the v flag, unescaped special characters inside classes are syntax errors.
Older browsers lack v flag, modifiers and RegExp.escape; feature-detect with try/new RegExp.

examples.title: Four modern regex features

interview.q: What does the v flag add over u?
interview.a: Set operations (subtraction and intersection) inside character classes, nested classes and properties of strings such as emoji sequences, with stricter syntax.

interview.q: Why use RegExp.escape?
interview.a: It escapes regex special characters in user-provided text so it matches literally and safely.

topics.title: using and Explicit Resource Management
topics.summary: Automatic cleanup with using and await using, Symbol.dispose, and DisposableStack. Stage 3 proposal, supported in Node 24 and Chrome 134+.
topics.description:
**Status (be careful):** Explicit Resource Management is a **TC39 Stage 3** proposal at the time of writing, not yet part of the ECMAScript spec. V8 ships it in **Chrome 134+ and Node 24**, and TypeScript 5.2+ and Babel can compile it. Firefox and Safari support is still arriving, so check before using it in browser code.

### The idea
A `using` declaration disposes a resource automatically when the block ends, whether it ends normally, by `return`, `break` or by throwing, like Python's `with` or C#'s `using`. It replaces `try/finally` boilerplate.

```js
{
  using file = openFile();       // calls file[Symbol.dispose]() at block exit
  await using db = await connect(); // calls db[Symbol.asyncDispose]()
}
```

### Pieces
| Piece | Role |
|---|---|
| `Symbol.dispose` | method name for sync cleanup |
| `Symbol.asyncDispose` | method name for async cleanup (awaited) |
| `using x = v` | block-scoped, `const`-like binding; `null`/`undefined` allowed |
| `await using x = v` | async disposal; allowed in async functions and modules |
| `DisposableStack` / `AsyncDisposableStack` | collect many cleanups: `use()`, `adopt()`, `defer()`, `dispose()` |
| `SuppressedError` | thrown when disposal fails while another error is propagating |

### Rules
- Resources dispose in **reverse order** of declaration.
- The value must have the dispose method, otherwise a `TypeError` is thrown at the declaration.
- Errors thrown by several disposers are combined into a `SuppressedError`.
- Great for locks, file handles, DB transactions, timers and temporary state (for example "disable logging until block end").
keyPoints: using disposes a resource at the end of its block, even on errors.
Implement [Symbol.dispose]() or [Symbol.asyncDispose]() on your objects.
Disposal order is the reverse of declaration order.
DisposableStack handles dynamic or many resources.
Stage 3 proposal; works in Node 24 and Chrome 134+, transpile elsewhere.
pitfalls: Assuming browser-wide support: Firefox and Safari lag behind.
using is block scoped; use it inside a function or block, not for module-lifetime values.

examples.title: Automatic cleanup in reverse order

interview.q: What does a using declaration do?
interview.a: It calls the object's Symbol.dispose method when the enclosing block exits, in reverse declaration order, even if an error is thrown.

interview.q: What is the standard status of using?
interview.a: A Stage 3 TC39 proposal shipped in V8 (Node 24, Chrome 134+); not yet in the ECMAScript spec or all browsers.

topics.title: Temporal: The Modern Date and Time API
topics.summary: Overview of Temporal, the immutable replacement for Date with time zones, calendars and exact durations, and how to use it today.
topics.description:
**Status:** Temporal is a TC39 proposal that has been at **Stage 3** for years. It has started shipping in browsers (Firefox first, then Chromium-based browsers) but is **not available in Node 24** (`typeof Temporal` is `'undefined'`). Check current support on caniuse/MDN, or use the `@js-temporal/polyfill` package. The examples below are therefore view-only.

### Why replace Date?
`Date` is mutable, zero-based for months, mixes local/UTC confusingly, has no real time-zone support and parses inconsistently. Temporal fixes all of that with **immutable** types and clear naming.

| Type | Represents |
|---|---|
| `Temporal.Instant` | exact moment (ns since epoch), no zone |
| `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` | instant + time zone + calendar (DST-aware) |
| `Temporal.PlainDate` | calendar date, no time or zone (birthdays) |
| `Temporal.PlainTime` | wall-clock time |
| `Temporal.PlainDateTime` | date + time without zone |
| `Temporal.PlainYearMonth` / `PlainMonthDay` | partial dates |
| `Temporal.Duration` | length of time (`P1Y2M3DT4H`) |
| `Temporal.Now` | current instant, zone, plain date |

### Main differences
- Months are **1-12**.
- Arithmetic returns new objects: `date.add({ months: 1 })`, `since()`, `until()`, `round()`.
- Comparisons with `Temporal.PlainDate.compare(a, b)` and `.equals()`.
- Parsing is strict ISO 8601 (with extensions), so invalid strings throw instead of guessing.
- Non-Gregorian calendars are supported (`calendar: 'hebrew'`).
- Time zone transitions (DST) are handled by `ZonedDateTime`, so "same wall time tomorrow" is correct.

### Today
Use `Date` plus `Intl.DateTimeFormat` for simple tasks, a polyfill or library (date-fns, Luxon) for complex time zone logic, and plan migration to Temporal.
keyPoints: Temporal types are immutable and months start at 1.
Instant is an exact moment; PlainDate has no zone; ZonedDateTime adds time zone and calendar.
Duration arithmetic and rounding are first-class operations.
Stage 3 and shipping in some browsers, not in Node 24; use a polyfill if needed.
Use feature detection: if (typeof Temporal !== 'undefined').
pitfalls: Do not assume Temporal exists in your target runtime without feature detection.
Mixing Temporal types requires explicit conversion (toPlainDate, toZonedDateTime).

examples.title: Temporal API sketch (view only)
examples.explanation: Not runnable on Node 24; use browsers that ship Temporal or the polyfill.

interview.q: Why was Temporal created?
interview.a: Date is mutable, has confusing zero-based months, weak time zone and parsing support; Temporal provides immutable types, explicit zones and calendars, and precise arithmetic.

interview.q: What is the difference between Instant and ZonedDateTime?
interview.a: Instant is an exact point in time without a zone; ZonedDateTime pairs that instant with a time zone and calendar so human-readable fields and DST rules apply.

topics.title: Import Attributes, JSON Modules and Top-level await
topics.summary: Load JSON with import ... with { type: 'json' }, plus top-level await in modules and dynamic import options.
topics.description:
### Import attributes (ES2025)
Syntax: `import data from './config.json' with { type: 'json' };`. The `with { ... }` clause passes **attributes** that tell the host how to treat the module. The standard attribute is `type: 'json'`, which lets you import JSON as a module safely (the response must be JSON, never executed as code).

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| Static import | `import cfg from './cfg.json' with { type: 'json' }` |
| Dynamic import | `const { default: cfg } = await import('./cfg.json', { with: { type: 'json' } })` |
| Re-export | `export { default } from './cfg.json' with { type: 'json' }` |

- Node 22+ supports it (Node 20 used the older `assert` keyword, now **removed**). Chrome 123+, Safari 17.2+, Firefox 138+.
- The JSON default export is a shared, parsed object; mutations affect all importers.
- CSS modules (`type: 'css'`) exist in some browsers; they are not part of the core language.

### Top-level await (ES2022)
In ES modules you can use `await` outside functions:

```js
const config = await fetch('/config.json').then(r => r.json());
export const api = new Client(config);
```
- The module becomes async; modules that import it **wait** for it to finish.
- It works only in modules (not classic scripts or CommonJS `require`).
- Great for configuration loading, optional dependencies and database connections; avoid slow awaits on the critical startup path.
- A rejected top-level await fails the whole module graph.

### Related
`import.meta.url`, `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` (Node 20.11+), and `import.meta.resolve()`.
keyPoints: import x from './f.json' with { type: 'json' } is the standard way to import JSON.
Dynamic import takes the same attributes in a second argument.
Top-level await works only in ES modules and delays importers until it resolves.
Node 20 used assert; modern code must use with.
Avoid long top-level awaits on startup paths.
pitfalls: Using the old assert keyword on Node 22+ fails; switch to with.
Top-level await in a CommonJS file is a SyntaxError.

examples.title: Modules with attributes and TLA
examples.explanation: Needs real module files (type: module or .mjs).

interview.q: How do you import a JSON file as an ES module?
interview.a: import data from './file.json' with { type: 'json' }; the with clause provides the import attribute.

interview.q: What does top-level await do to modules that import the awaiting module?
interview.a: They wait until its top-level await completes before they start executing.

topics.title: Decorators Overview
topics.summary: What the standard decorator proposal does, the syntax, current support status and the difference from TypeScript's legacy decorators.
topics.description:
**Status (honest summary):** The standard decorators proposal is **TC39 Stage 3**. TypeScript 5.0+ (without `experimentalDecorators`), Babel (`@babel/plugin-proposal-decorators`) and some bundlers implement it. **Node 24 and most browsers do not run decorators natively**, so the examples below are view-only and need a compiler. Always check the current proposal stage before relying on native support.

### What is a decorator?
A function that wraps or replaces a class element **at definition time**, written with `@` before the element. It receives the original value and a `context` object and may return a replacement.

```js
function logged(value, context) {
  if (context.kind === 'method') {
    return function (...args) { console.log(`call ${context.name}`); return value.apply(this, args); };
  }
}
class Api { @logged fetchUser(id) { /* ... */ } }
```

### What can be decorated?
| Target | `context.kind` | Return |
|---|---|---|
| Class | `'class'` | new class or nothing |
| Method | `'method'` | replacement function |
| Getter / setter | `'getter'` / `'setter'` | replacement function |
| Field | `'field'` | initializer wrapper `(initial) => newInitial` |
| `accessor x` (auto-accessor) | `'accessor'` | `{ get, set, init }` |

`context` also provides `name`, `static`, `private`, `access` and `addInitializer(fn)`. Decorators can take arguments by being factories: `@retry(3)`.

### Differences from legacy TypeScript decorators
The old `experimentalDecorators` used a different signature `(target, key, descriptor)` and powered Angular and NestJS. The standard version has no parameter decorators yet, and it is **not** compatible with the legacy one; frameworks migrate gradually.

### Use cases
Logging, timing, validation, memoization, dependency injection metadata, event binding and reactive state (for example MobX and Lit use decorators heavily).
keyPoints: Decorators are Stage 3 and need a compiler (TypeScript 5+, Babel) today.
The syntax is @name placed before a class, method, getter, setter, field or accessor.
A decorator receives (value, context) and can return a replacement.
Legacy TypeScript decorators (experimentalDecorators) have a different API.
Decorator factories take arguments, like @retry(3).
pitfalls: Mixing legacy and standard decorators in the same project causes confusing errors.
Decorators are not natively supported in Node 24, so a plain node file with @ fails to parse.

examples.title: A method decorator with a factory (view only)
examples.explanation: Compile with TypeScript 5+ or Babel to run.

interview.q: What arguments does a standard method decorator receive?
interview.a: The original method (value) and a context object describing kind, name, static, private status and utilities such as addInitializer.

interview.q: Can you use decorators in Node.js without a compiler?
interview.a: Not natively at the time of writing (Node 24); use TypeScript 5+, Babel or a bundler plugin.

topics.title: Small Modern Gems: Error.cause, hasOwn, structuredClone, hashbang, at and more
topics.summary: Handy features from ES2019 to ES2025 that are easy to miss: Error cause, Object.hasOwn, structuredClone, findLast, hashbang, AggregateError, Error.isError and more.
topics.description:
A tour of small but useful features, all runnable on Node 24 unless noted.

| Feature | Version | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `new Error(msg, { cause })` | ES2022 | chain the underlying error |
| `Object.hasOwn(o, k)` | ES2022 | safe own-property check |
| `arr.at(-1)`, `str.at(-1)` | ES2022 | negative indexing |
| Class static blocks, `#x in obj` | ES2022 | advanced class features |
| `structuredClone(v)` | web platform / Node 17+ | deep copy supporting cycles, Date, Map, Set |
| `Array.prototype.findLast` | ES2023 | search from the end |
| Hashbang `#!/usr/bin/env node` | ES2023 | first line allowed in scripts and modules |
| `str.replaceAll`, `Promise.any`, `AggregateError` | ES2021 | |
| Logical assignment `??=` | ES2021 | |
| Numeric separators `1_000` | ES2021 | |
| `WeakRef`, `FinalizationRegistry` | ES2021 | weak references |
| `Object.fromEntries`, `flat`, `flatMap`, `trimStart` | ES2019 | |
| Optional catch binding `catch {}` | ES2019 | |
| `BigInt`, dynamic `import()`, `?.` / `??` | ES2020 | |
| `Error.isError(v)` | recent (V8 13.4+) | reliable error brand check across realms |
| `Float16Array`, `Math.f16round` | ES2025 | half-precision floats |
| `JSON.rawJSON` | recent | write exact number text into JSON |
| Duplicate named groups, `Promise.try` | ES2025 | covered in other topics |

### Error cause
Use `cause` to keep the original error when you add context: `throw new Error('Cannot load profile', { cause: err })`. Logs and DevTools display the chain.

### Not available yet (Node 24)
`Uint8Array.fromBase64`, `Math.sumPrecise`, `Map.prototype.getOrInsert`, async iterator helpers and `Temporal` are newer additions or proposals; always feature-detect before using them.
keyPoints: Error cause preserves the original exception while adding context.
Object.hasOwn replaces hasOwnProperty.call and works on null-prototype objects.
structuredClone is the built-in deep clone.
findLast, at, and replaceAll round out the standard library.
A hashbang line lets scripts be run directly as CLI tools.
pitfalls: structuredClone cannot copy functions or class prototypes.
Check engine support before using features from the last two years.

interview.q: What is Error cause used for?
interview.a: To attach the original error to a new, more descriptive error, preserving the chain for debugging.

interview.q: Why prefer Object.hasOwn over obj.hasOwnProperty?
interview.a: It works for objects without a prototype and cannot be shadowed by an own property named hasOwnProperty.

topics.title: Well-formed Strings, Resizable ArrayBuffer, transfer and Atomics.waitAsync
topics.summary: ES2024 additions for binary and concurrent data: isWellFormed/toWellFormed, resizable and transferable ArrayBuffers, and non-blocking Atomics.waitAsync.
topics.description:
All features in this topic are **ES2024** and run on Node 22+ and current browsers.

### Well-formed strings
JavaScript strings are UTF-16; a **lone surrogate** (half of an emoji pair) is invalid Unicode. `str.isWellFormed()` returns `false` if one exists and `str.toWellFormed()` replaces each with U+FFFD. This avoids `URIError` from `encodeURIComponent` and corrupt data when sending text to APIs that require valid Unicode.

### Resizable ArrayBuffer
`new ArrayBuffer(8, { maxByteLength: 64 })` creates a buffer you can grow with `buf.resize(n)`. Properties: `resizable`, `maxByteLength`. TypedArrays created **without a fixed length** track the buffer ("length-tracking"). `SharedArrayBuffer` has the growable equivalent `grow(n)`. Useful for streaming parsers and avoiding copies.

### transfer()
`buf.transfer(newLength?)` moves the contents into a **new** ArrayBuffer and detaches the old one (its `byteLength` becomes 0, `detached` is `true`). `transferToFixedLength()` returns a non-resizable copy. It makes zero-copy hand-offs between workers explicit and efficient.

### Atomics.waitAsync
`Atomics.wait` blocks a thread, which is forbidden on the browser main thread. `Atomics.waitAsync(int32Array, index, expected, timeout)` returns `{ async, value }` where `value` is a promise (when `async` is true) that resolves `"ok"` after `Atomics.notify`, or `"timed-out"`. If the value differs immediately it returns `{ async: false, value: "not-equal" }`. It lets the main thread coordinate with workers over `SharedArrayBuffer` without freezing the UI (browsers need cross-origin isolation for SharedArrayBuffer).

### Related
`Float16Array` and `Math.f16round` (ES2025), `Atomics.pause` is newer and not yet universal.
keyPoints: isWellFormed detects lone surrogates; toWellFormed replaces them with U+FFFD.
Resizable ArrayBuffer uses maxByteLength and resize().
transfer() moves data to a new buffer and detaches the original.
Atomics.waitAsync returns a promise instead of blocking the thread.
SharedArrayBuffer in browsers needs cross-origin isolation.
pitfalls: A detached ArrayBuffer cannot be used again; typed array views on it become length 0.
Resizing shrinks views silently; length-tracking views change length automatically.

interview.q: What does ArrayBuffer.prototype.transfer do?
interview.a: It creates a new buffer with the same contents (optionally resized) and detaches the original so it can no longer be used.

interview.q: Why was Atomics.waitAsync added?
interview.a: Atomics.wait blocks the thread and is disallowed on the browser main thread; waitAsync returns a promise so the main thread can wait for a worker notification without freezing.
